title: The Principle of Rebirth
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The principle of rebirth: right mindfulness at the moment of death, which invites the Buddha's coming to welcome.

inline.s: The principle of rebirth: right mindfulness at the moment of death, which invites the Buddha's coming to welcome.
Q: What is the principle of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Answer: The principle of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is:
right mindfulness at death, which invites the Buddha's coming to welcome.
Master Lianchi (Zhuhong) says:
“Within, focus the mind on right mindfulness; without, sense the Buddha's coming to welcome.”
(from the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra)
[Right mindfulness at death, inviting the Buddha's coming to welcome] At the moment of death, maintain
the Buddha-recitation's
right mindfulness, and be in mutual resonance (gǎnyìng) with the Buddha, so that the Buddha comes to receive and guide. Therefore Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, instructs:
“When it is sustained, one is reborn”
(at death, so long as one's Buddha-recitation thought is sustained without being cut off by stray thoughts, one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Both Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo instruct:
if the ten recitations at death are sustained, one will be reborn.
(For details see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
, and
Master Daochuo's Pure Practice Teachings

As for the case of those who at death are upside-down, without right mindfulness, and who, drawn along by the force of karma, are reborn in the corresponding destiny among the six paths (rebirth in accord with karma),
Master Lianchi
instructs

“Those who are upside-down at death — because they used to follow after deluded thoughts and did not cultivate right mindfulness, their minds were scattered. At the moment of leaving the warm touch (of the body), all the deeds of a lifetime appear before them, and their spirits are terrified and their movements wild. Those who should enter hell see the mountain of knives and the forest of swords as a garden. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey as a palace. Even those who have done good and should be born among humans or gods cannot help loving and hating their parents. Even lesser sages at their initial resolve cannot rightly know their entering and leaving. All these are what are called being upside-down. Through this upside-down state, within the three realms and the seven destinies,
they are reborn according to karma
(from the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra)

Translation: Those who are upside-down at death, because they used to follow after deluded thoughts and did not cultivate right mindfulness, have scattered minds. When the four great elements dissolve, all the deeds of a lifetime appear before them, their spirits are terrified, and their movements are confounded. Those who should enter hell take the mountain of knives and the forest of swords to be a beautiful garden. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse and the belly of a donkey to be a splendid hall. Even those who have done good and should be born in the human or heavenly path, upon entering the womb, cannot help loving the mother and hating the father to be born male, or loving the father and hating the mother to be born female. Even the lesser sages of the first stage (of the Śrāvaka path) and bodhisattvas of initial resolve still have the delusion of the intervening birth (géyīn zhī mí) and cannot rightly know entering and leaving the womb. These are all the so-called upside-down states. Through this upside-down state at death, in the seven destinies within the three realms, they are reborn according to karma.
[Seven destinies] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, spirit immortals, gods, and asuras. “Destiny” (qù) means a going, a direction.
The Zhongfeng Three-Fold Contemplation (Zhongfeng Sanshi Xinian) says:

“Yet although it is said that Amitābha gathers in sentient beings for rebirth, one must believe that it is only manifested in accord with one's own mind, an interpenetration of response and resonance; ultimately it is not obtained from without.”

[Only manifested in accord with one's own mind] The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When the water of the mind is clear (still and clear), the Buddha-moon appears; when the water of the mind is stirred and muddy (in motion and muddy), though the Buddha-moon shines, its reflection is not clearly seen. [Interpenetration of response and resonance] The response (the sense) of sentient beings and the resonance (the response) of Amitābha Buddha interpenetrate each other.
Master Yinguang, speaking of the principle of mutual resonance at the time of death, says:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have complete faith and vows and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and sincere, and accords with greed, anger, and delusion, turning away from the Buddha, it is like water that is muddy and moving; though the moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners)

This says: The minds of sentient beings are like pools of water; Amitābha Buddha is like the bright moon in the sky. When sentient beings at death sense the Buddha with right mindfulness, the Buddha responds; if the pool of water is clear and still, the bright moon's reflection appears within it. This is a metaphor: right mindfulness at death senses and manifests Amitābha Buddha's coming to welcome. If at the moment of death the mind is not pure, not sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like a pool of muddy, agitated water; though the bright moon in the sky does not fail to shine upon it, the moon cannot be clearly reflected in that pool. This is a metaphor: an agitated, muddy, deluded mind at death cannot sense and manifest Amitābha Buddha's coming to receive and guide.
Concerning
the single thought conditioned at death
, Master Chewu instructs:
[The single thought conditioned at death] The thought, at the moment of death, that determines where the consciousness (shénshí) goes to be reborn.

“Our present single thought is conditioned and without self-nature, and without self-nature it is conditioned. If one does not give birth to the Buddha-realm, one gives birth to one of the nine realms. If we take it as conditioned and without self-nature, then sentient beings and Buddha are equally one emptiness. If we take it as without self-nature and conditioned, then the ten realms differ vastly in excellence and inferiority. King Aśoka, at his death, because a fly-whisking servant brushed his face with a whisk, gave rise to a single thought of anger and fell to become a venomous snake. A woman fording a river slipped, and her child fell into the water; because she reached for the child, she sank with it. Because of her mind of compassion, she was reborn in heaven. Since a single thought of compassion or anger at once divides heaven from the animals, should one not be careful with this single thought conditioned at death? If with this mind one turns to the thought of Amitābha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?”

Translation: Our present single thought is conditioned and without self-nature; without self-nature it is conditioned. If one does not give birth to the Buddha-realm, one gives birth to one of the nine realms. If we take it as conditioned and without self-nature, then sentient beings and the Buddha are equal, both being one emptiness. If we take it as without self-nature and conditioned, then among the ten realms the excellence or inferiority is very vast. When King Aśoka was dying, a fly-whisking servant happened to brush his face with a fan, and a single thought of anger arose; because this dying thought was one of anger, he fell to become a venomous snake. A woman fording a river slipped, and her child fell into the water; because she went to save the child, both she and the child were drowned. Because her dying thought was one of compassion, this woman was reborn in heaven. A dying thought of compassion or anger — the compassionate one is born in heaven, the angry one is born an animal, so that excellence and inferiority are at once divided — how can one fail to be cautious with this single dying thought conditioned at death? If at death with this mind one turns to the thought of Amitābha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?

[Without self-nature] “Dharmas have no self-nature” means that all dharmas have no real substance; they are all illusions, like things in a dream. Without self-nature is also called no-nature. The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says: “All dharmas are without self-nature.” The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that dharmas are ever without self-nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without self-nature.” [Nine realms] Among the ten realms, the other nine besides the Buddha-realm. [Ten realms] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddha. The first six are the six ordinary states; the last four are the four sages. [King Aśoka] King Aśoka (Aqídá wáng), who in his life built countless stupas, made offerings to the Three Jewels, upheld the true Dharma, and had vast merit. At the moment of death, because his attendant carelessly brushed his face with a fan, he gave rise to a thought of anger and fell to become a venomous snake. The matter appears in the Scripture of Miscellaneous Parables.

“But this single thought cannot be had by mere luck. One must hold it with sincerity and maintain it through constant practice. Therefore we who practice this single phrase Amitābha, reciting it a thousand times and ten thousand times, even all day and all year, do so only to mature this single thought. If one single thought is fully matured, then at the moment of death there is only this thought, with no other thought besides. Master Zhiyi says: ‘The mind that is in concentration at death is the mind that is reborn in the Pure Land.’ Now if there is only this thought and no other thought, is it not the mind in concentration? If the thought is truly so, and one does not see Amitābha, whom else would one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else would one be reborn? I only fear that we do not have enough faith in ourselves.
(from the Collected Works of Master Chewu)

Translation: But this single dying thought cannot be had by mere luck. One must hold it with sincerity and maintain it through constant practice. Therefore we, practicing this single phrase Amitābha, reciting it a thousand times, ten thousand times, even all day and all year, do so only to mature this single thought of Buddha-recitation, so as to ensure that the dying thought is one of reciting Amitābha. If the single thought of Buddha-recitation is truly fully matured, then at the moment of death there is only this thought of Buddha-recitation, with no other thought. Master Zhiyi says: ‘The mind in concentration at death is the mind that is reborn in the Pure Land.’ If there is only the thought of Buddha-recitation and no other thought, is that not a mind in concentration? Since at death one is in a mind of concentration, if one does not see Amitābha, whom else would one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else would one be reborn? I only fear that we have not truly believed in the principle above. If we truly believed, how could we fail to strive to mature this single thought of Buddha-recitation and be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?

[To mature this single thought] One must achieve what Mahasthamaprapta calls “pure thought continuing unbroken,” which is also what Master Shandao (the second Patriarch of the Pure Land school) calls “thought after thought sustained.” (Note: “thought after thought sustained” means the thought of Buddha-recitation sustained from one thought to the next, not the case of reciting Amitābha aloud with the mouth while the mind wanders in delusion.) Master Shandao says: “Therefore the Great Sage (Śākyamuni Buddha), with compassion, directly urges exclusive recitation of the Name; precisely because the recitation of the Name is easy, when it is sustained one is reborn. If one can sustain it thought after thought for the whole of life till death, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn. … I wish that all people would think this over well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, they must rouse their minds and restrain themselves, not letting up by day or night; the last thought at the end of life, and the next thought, is reborn; forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, up to the attainment of Buddhahood — how delightful!”
(For details see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
So, sustaining the thought day after day is the guarantee of clear right mindfulness at death; and clear right mindfulness at death is the key to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Of the principle of resonance in “at death, within focus the mind on right mindfulness, without sense the Buddha's coming to welcome,” Master Yinguang has an incisive passage in his Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners, which I now transcribe and annotate below:

“Someone says: Amitābha Buddha dwells at ease in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable and boundless. The sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name in a single world are likewise immeasurable and boundless. How can Amitābha Buddha, with one body, at one time universally receive and guide all the reciting sentient beings of the immeasurable and boundless worlds of the ten directions?”

Someone asks: Amitābha Buddha dwells at ease in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Yet the worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable and boundless, and the sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name in a single world are likewise immeasurable and boundless. How can Amitābha Buddha, with this one body, in a single moment, universally receive and guide all the reciting sentient beings of the immeasurable and boundless worlds of the ten directions?

“Answer: How can you, with the views of an ordinary man, speculate on the realm of the Buddha? Let me use a simile to make it clear and dispel your doubt. A single moon shines in the sky, and its reflection appears in ten thousand streams — does the moon take any thought to do so?”

Answer: How can you, with the views of an ordinary man, speculate on the realm of the Buddha? (The frog at the bottom of a well — how can it know there are still mountains, rivers, oceans, and towns?) Let me use a simile to explain and rid you of your doubt. A single bright moon hangs high in the sky, and its reflection appears in ten thousand rivers and streams — yet does the bright moon deliberately shine on this river or that?

“Now in the sky there is only one moon, and yet the great sea, the great rivers, the great streams, and the small brooks all reflect the full moon. Even in so small a thing as a single ladle or a drop of water, the full moon is always reflected in full.”

In the sky there is only one moon, and yet the great sea, the great rivers, the great streams, and the small brooks all reflect the full moon. Even down to a ladle or a drop of water, in each the full moon is reflected in full.

“… Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is muddy and moving it is hidden. The moon itself has no choosing and rejecting; where it does not appear, it is because the water is dim, muddy, and rushing, and so unable to receive its reflection.”

… However, only when the water is clear and still does the moon appear; when the water is muddy and moving, the moon is hidden. The moon indeed has no choosing or rejecting (the bright moon does not deliberately shine on some waters and not on others); where it does not appear, it is because the water is dim, muddy, and rushing, unable to receive its reflection. (So where a moon-reflection does not appear in some water, the fault lies not with the moon [“that land does not turn away”] but with the water [“it is drawn by its own nature”]. The Sukhāvatīvyūha Sutra, the Sutra of Amitāyus (Foshuo Wuliangshou Jing), says: “Rising to the Way is without limit or end, easy to go to, yet no one goes; that land does not turn away, but [sentient beings] are drawn by their own nature.”)

[That land does not turn away; it is drawn by its own nature] The Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss does not reject any sentient being (that land does not turn away), but the reason sentient beings cannot be reborn there is that at death they cannot maintain right mindfulness and the intermediate states (yīnjìng) appear, and so they follow the force of karma to be reborn in the six destinies, utterly unable to be their own masters (drawn by their own nature).

“The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have faith and vows complete, and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like water that is muddy and moving; though the moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested.”

The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have complete faith and vows and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear and still the moon appears (a metaphor: the pure mind of right mindfulness senses Amitābha Buddha's coming to receive and guide). If the mind is not pure, not sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like muddied, agitated water; though the Buddha-moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested (a metaphor: an agitated, muddy, deluded mind cannot sense Amitābha Buddha's coming to receive and guide).

“The moon is but a form-dharma of the world, and yet it has such wonder. How much more so Amitābha Buddha, who has utterly purified afflictions and delusions, is complete in merit and wisdom, whose mind encompasses the great emptiness, whose measure extends throughout the dharma-realm? Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘The Buddha's body fills the dharma-realm, manifesting everywhere before all sentient beings; responding to conditions it never fails to reach them, while ever dwelling on this bodhi-seat.’ Hence we know that the response pervades the dharma-realm, and the resonance pervades the dharma-realm. The Buddha has truly never stirred his mind or thought, nor has any mark of coming or going, and yet he can cause sentient beings whose conditions are ripe to see him come here to receive and guide them to the West.”

The moon is but a form-dharma of the world and yet has such wonder. How much more so Amitābha Buddha, who has utterly purified afflictions and delusions, is complete in merit and wisdom, whose mind encompasses the great emptiness and whose measure extends throughout the dharma-realm? Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: “The Buddha's body fills the dharma-realm, manifesting everywhere before all sentient beings; responding to conditions it never fails to reach them, while ever dwelling on this bodhi-seat.” Hence we know: sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm respond (sense), and Amitābha Buddha throughout the dharma-realm resonates. Amitābha Buddha has truly never stirred his mind or thought, never had any mark of coming or going, and yet he can cause sentient beings whose conditions are ripe to see him come here to receive and guide them to the West.
The Sutra of Praising the Merit of the Buddhas says:
“When life is about to end, if one has single-minded faith and joy, with a thought that does not forget or abandon, Amitābha Buddha, leading
(bringing)
the assembly of monks
(Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas)
, stands before that person; the māras can never destroy this
(this person's)
mind of right awakening.”
Master Xing'an (the eleventh Patriarch of the Pure Land school) says:

“Suppose one is upside-down in a single thought at death — not only will one not be born in the nine grades, one can scarcely avoid the three lower paths; though the Buddha is greatly compassionate, he cannot save me. Alas! Alas!”
(from the Debate on Demonic Possession in Reciting the Buddha's Name)
Master Yinguang says:
“At the time of death, by one's own pure mind, one senses the Buddha's receiving and guidance to be reborn in the West.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Reply to the Layman Gu Zongkuang)
Master Yinguang, speaking of the principle of Amitābha Buddha's receiving and guiding sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name at the time of death, says:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have faith and vows complete, and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like water that is muddy and moving; though the moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners)

Therefore Master Yinguang, in his Three Essentials at the Time of Death, instructs: “Now I set forth the three essentials as the basis for helping the dying attain rebirth. Though the words are plain and vulgar, the meaning is from the Buddha's scriptures; when encountering this occasion, put them all into practice. The three essentials are: first, skillfully guide and comfort, to give rise to right faith; second, all present should take turns reciting the Buddha's name to aid the pure mindfulness; third, strictly refrain from moving the body and from weeping, to prevent mishaps.” These three essentials are all to cause the dying to give rise to right mindfulness, to gather it, to maintain it, and to sense the Buddha's coming to welcome.

The questioner says: The view that “right mindfulness at death and the Buddha's coming to welcome” is correct — rather, “the Buddha's coming to welcome, and one abides in right mindfulness,” is right.

Master Hōnen says: “Moreover, one who truly has the resolve for rebirth, who believes in Amitābha's primal vow and recites the Buddha's name — such a person is not upside-down at death. The reason is that the Buddha's coming to welcome is precisely for the sake of the practitioner's right mindfulness at death. Those who do not understand this all think that it is their own right mindfulness at death and [that only when] reciting does the Buddha come to welcome; this view repudiates the primal vow and also does not know the scriptures. The Sutra of Praising the Pure Land says: ‘
Compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused.’

“When one constantly recites [the Buddha's name] in daily life, the Buddha will surely come to welcome; once one sees the Buddha appear, one abides in right mindfulness. Therefore do not think that reciting is in vain, and [do not think] that merely praying for right mindfulness at death is correct — such a view is very mistaken. Hence one who believes in Amitābha's primal vow must not harbor doubt about the mind at death. Even for one who only recites at the time of death, Amitābha also made the vow to come and welcome. One who attains rebirth by reciting at death — originally he had no vow for rebirth, but was an evil being given over to sin; at the moment of death, encountering a good companion's urging, he recites and is reborn — the Contemplation Sutra also speaks of this. If one is a person of constant recitation, one need not forcefully judge the marks at death. Because the Buddha's coming to welcome is certain, the right mindfulness at death is likewise certain; this principle should be borne in mind.””
Answer: In the Sutra of Praising the Pure Land (
the Sutra of Praising the Buddha's Reception of the Pure Land
), the passage “compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused” runs:

“If there are pure-hearted good men or good women who, having heard the immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable name of merit of Amitāyus Buddha and the merit and adornment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, reflect upon it after hearing — for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven,
with thought not confused (single-mindedness)
. If
(this)
good man or good woman, at the moment of death, [with] Amitāyus Buddha together with his immeasurable Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding front and back,
comes and stands before him
, with compassion and aid,
causing the mind not to be confused

. Once life has been laid down, following the Buddha's assembly, he is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus.” The World-Honored One here clearly instructs: the good man or good woman who, in reciting the Buddha's name, keeps the thought not confused
(single-mindedness)

, “at the moment of death, [with] Amitāyus Buddha together with his immeasurable Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding front and back, comes and stands before him, with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused.”
Therefore the premise of the Buddha's
“coming to stand before him, with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused”
is that this dying person has already attained thought-not-confused (single-mindedness)
Therefore the World-Honored One in this sutra says: reciting the Buddha's name to reach thought-not-confused (single-mindedness), the Buddha
will surely
come to welcome. Yet Master Hōnen twisted the text into: “When one constantly recites in daily life, the Buddha
will surely

come to welcome.” And then he rebukes: “Those who do not understand this all think it is their own right mindfulness at death when reciting that the Buddha comes to welcome; this view repudiates the primal vow and also does not know the scriptures.” May I ask: who, in the end, is the one who does not know the scriptures?
Q: Since “this good man or good woman” has already attained thought not confused, why does it say that after Amitābha Buddha comes, “with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused”?

Answer: Thought not confused is what senses the Buddha's coming to welcome, but thought not confused is a shallower level of practice, often not enough to keep the mind from confusion at the time when the four great elements dissolve and suffering presses and demons appear, and that is why Amitābha Buddha “with compassion and aid causes the mind not to be confused.” The Sutra of Praising the Merit of the Buddhas says:
“When life is about to end, with single-minded faith and joy, with a thought that does not forget or abandon
this is right mindfulness at death
, Amitābha Buddha, leading
(bringing)
the assembly of monks
(Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas)
, stands before that person; the māras can never destroy this
(this good man or good woman's)
mind of right awakening.”

Moreover, in this sutra (the Sutra of Praising the Pure Land), after speaking of thought not confused (single-mindedness), the World-Honored One emphasizes again and again, over and over, the requirement to
practice as taught
. The “practice as taught” spoken of here means that faith, vows, and the holding of the Name must attain thought not confused (single-mindedness). And he clearly tells us:
only by practicing as taught

is one received and embraced by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and will surely be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and will never withdraw, quickly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood — his concern overflowing in the words. How could it be that merely having faith suffices for “at the moment of death, [with] Amitāyus Buddha together with his immeasurable Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding front and back, comes and stands before him, with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused”?
The World-Honored One instructs:

“If there are pure-hearted good men or good women, who have heard such inconceivable merit of the Name of Amitāyus Buddha and the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all believe, receive, and make the vow,
practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha-land.”

“Those who practice as taught will all, for certain, be irrevocable from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and will all, for certain, be born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha. Therefore, Śāriputra, all you sentient beings should believe, accept, and comprehend the words of me and the Buddhas of the ten directions, and diligently progress,
practicing as taught
, without giving rise to doubt.”
Those who practice as taught

, all for certain, from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi are irrevocable; all for certain are born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha. Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are pure-hearted good men or good women, they should all, with deep mind, believe and understand the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus, make the vow for rebirth,
and not be given to negligence

“In this defiled world of endurance, in the time of the five turbidities, if there are pure-hearted good men or good women, who, having heard this most-difficult-to-believe Dharma of all the world, can give rise to faith and understanding, and receive, uphold, expound, and
practice as taught

, know that such a person is most rare, having planted good roots in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas. At the end of life, such a person will surely be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and enjoy the various meritorious adornments of the pure Buddha-land and the Mahāyāna bliss of the Dharma.”

As for the case in the Contemplation Sutra of “evil beings given over to past sins who, at the time of death, first encounter a good companion's urging and recite [the Buddha's name]” and so attain rebirth, Master Yinguang says:

“The Contemplation Sutra [speaks of] the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds; when about to die, the marks of hell appear. There is a good companion (original note: this does not distinguish monk or lay, man or woman; whoever can teach that person to recite [the Buddha's name] is called a good companion) who teaches him to recite the Buddha's name — perhaps only ten recitations, perhaps not even ten — and he directly dies, and still, relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, is reborn while carrying his karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have a fierce and urgent force utterly different as heaven from the abyss, and that is why he is reborn. Driven by the extreme suffering of hell, the instant he hears the Buddha's name, he recites it with his entire being.
Apart from this recitation, there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness, his mind is nonetheless without any different thought.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Reply to the Layman Chen Xinru.) Moreover, for such a person so able to be reborn, Master Ouyi adds:
“This is one in ten thousand; how could one depend on luck!”
(from the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra)

The questioner says: Master Taixu, in his Principle of Rebirth through Reciting the Buddha's Name, says: “Relying on the power of the good Dharma is faith; resolving to be reborn is the power of vows. If faith and vows are truly determined and firm, then whether the practice is shallow or deep, one can be reborn; it is only that with deeper practice the grade is higher.” So, as long as faith and vows are truly determined and firm, whether the practice is shallow or deep, one can be reborn.

Answer: Among faith, vows, and practice, the purpose of practice is to make faith and vows truly determined and firm, so that at the moment of death one can attain clear right mindfulness, and thereby ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Can the absence of practice, or shallow practice, achieve this? The Buddha in the scriptures repeatedly warns to “practice as taught,” and the patriarchs repeatedly say “by practice fulfill vows; by practice authenticate faith.” Why always tear practice apart from faith and vows, and speak of practice as if it were of no consequence? (Think deeply!) As if, apart from diligent, strenuous, vigorous recitation, one could make faith and vows truly determined and firm and have clear right mindfulness at death. Does this accord with the Buddha's words, the patriarchs' words, and the actual situation? In truth, I need not wait until death: even now you may test it. Can you, in joy or in anger, maintain clear right mindfulness? By this you can discern whether your faith and vows are truly determined and firm, and where you will go at the time of death.

Q: Master Taixu, in his Principle of Rebirth through Reciting the Buddha's Name, says: “The power of vows — the power of the vow-force — is inconceivable: it is the extremely sincere will-power produced by concentrating the mind's force. As when a person who recites the Buddha's name makes the vow for rebirth: at that moment making the vow, concentrating the mind's force on the vow for rebirth, over time maturing it, achieving the vow-force formed by practice — from the function accomplished by this vow-force, one can discover a result beyond the ordinary, produced by a conceivable causal force.” Does not “concentrating the mind's force on the vow for rebirth and, over time, maturing it” — with such firm faith and vows — surely entail rebirth?

Answer: “Concentrating the mind's force on the vow for rebirth and, over time, maturing it” — this IS practice, and very vigorous practice; and the conclusion in the same passage, “whether the practice is shallow or deep,” is self-contradictory with this. May I ask: can a shallow practice achieve “maturing over time”? You can verify this yourself.

The questioner says: Master Taixu, in his Principle of Rebirth through Reciting the Buddha's Name, says: “Even if one has not achieved good roots, so long as one believes in the power of the good Dharma, together with the earnest power of vows in one's own mind, one thereby achieves good roots, and can interpenetrate with the power of Amitābha Buddha's vows; what the power of Amitābha Buddha's vows accomplishes becomes what one's own vow-power accomplishes, and one can claim a share in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Here is a very ordinary example: suppose a rich man makes a will leaving all his property to aid the disabled throughout the whole world. If at that moment there is a person who is already disabled, then this person has a share in the rich man's bequeathed property. One who vows for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss thereby has a share in the Land — it is just the same.”

Answer: In the chapter on the Perfect Penetration through Reciting the Buddha's Name by Mahasthamaprapta, he, too, offers a simile. Suppose there are two men, A and B. A directs his whole mind to thinking of B, while B does not think of A at all. Such two people — even if they meet, it is as if they had not met; perhaps they see each other, and it is as if they had not seen. If both direct their whole minds to thinking of each other, then their thoughts of longing grow deeper and deeper, engraved into their very bones, so that from life to life, in life after life, for generation after generation, they are inseparable as shadow from form, of one feeling and one body, never apart or abandoned. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, compassionately loving and thinking of sentient beings, are like a mother thinking of her child. If the child runs away, though the mother thinks of him, what use is such constant longing to the child? If the child thinks of his mother as the mother thinks of him, then mother and child, from life to life, are neither adverse nor far apart. If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name until the practice matures into one, then in the present or the future they will surely see the Buddha, not far from Buddhahood; without relying on any other means, the mind will open of itself. (The original text:

“It is like a person — one wholly recollecting, the other wholly forgetting; such two people, if they meet it is as if they had not met, or if they see, it is as if they had not seen. If the two recollect each other, their recollections grow deep, until from life to life they are like shadow and form, never diverging. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, compassionately thinking of sentient beings, are like a mother thinking of her child; if the child runs away, though the mother thinks of him, what use is it? If the child thinks of his mother as the mother thinks of him, then mother and child, from life to life, are neither adverse nor far apart. If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, in the present or the future they will surely see the Buddha, not far from Buddhahood; without relying on means, the mind will open of itself.”
) Which of the two similes do you think is appropriate?

As for the principle of certain rebirth, and how certain rebirth is to be accomplished, the Buddha sets it out with perfect clarity in the Sutra of Praising the Buddha's Reception of the Pure Land. In that sutra Śākyamuni Buddha reveals the
dharma-gate of certain rebirth
in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, the
dharma-gate of liberation in this very life

. This dharma-gate is praised with one voice by the Buddhas of the ten directions. Those who give rise to deep faith and understanding will certainly be received and embraced by the Buddhas of the ten directions; those who practice as taught will certainly be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The sutra says:
(the Buddhas of the ten directions)
each manifest the mark of the broad and long tongue, which covers the three thousand great thousand worlds, and, encircling them round about, speak these words of truth: You sentient beings,
should all believe and accept
this 'praise of the inconceivable merit of the Buddha-land, the dharma-gate of reception
embraced by all the Buddhas
It also says:
"If a good man or good woman, having already heard, or being about to hear, or now hearing, this sutra, gives rise to deep faith and understanding upon hearing it,
having given rise to faith and understanding
he will certainly be
received and embraced by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who dwell in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges rivers
Practicing as taught
, he will in every case
certainly
attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi without retrogression, and in every case
certainly be born
in the pure Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life"

We should strictly follow the sutra text of the Sutra of Praising the Buddha's Reception of the Pure Land: accept it in faith, give rise to the vow, practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha-land. The sutra says:

"Contemplating such a great matter of benefit, peace, and happiness, I speak these words of truth: if there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear of this inconceivable name of merit of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and of the pure Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all
accept it in faith, give rise to the vow, practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha-land
Therefore, when studying and practicing, one who recites the Buddha's name must rely on the sutra text of the
Sutra of Praising the Buddha's Reception of the Pure Land
to see clearly the essential nature of the various divergent teachings, and walk unswervingly on the right path.
Do not, by any means, ruin your own great matter of rebirth!
Question: How can one, at the moment of death, gather right mindfulness within and sense the Buddha's welcome without?
Answer: The greatest obstruction to gathering right mindfulness within is delusive thoughts. In the practical training textbook of the Online Buddhist Academy of Practicing as Taught,
Aware Recitation of the Buddha

the causes of delusive thoughts are analyzed in detail, together with how to overcome them effectively; and the concrete steps and methods for reaching single-minded Buddha-recitation (unconfused mindfulness) are explained in detail as well. So long as one has true faith and an earnest vow, works hard and with diligence, advances step by step, and perseveres, one will certainly be able to reach single-minded Buddha-recitation (unconfused mindfulness), and at the moment of death gather right mindfulness within and sense the Buddha's welcome without.
